title: Ὄνος καὶ κηπωρός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 273. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ὑπηρετούμενος κηπωρῷ, ἐπειδὴ ὀλίγα μὲν ἤσθιε, πλεῖστα δ’ ἐμόχθει, ηὔξατο τῷ Διὶ ὥστε τοῦ κηπωροῦ ἀπαλλαγεὶς ἑτέρῳ ἀπεμποληθῆναι δεσπότῃ.
sentences.tr: Onos hypēretoumenos kēpōrōi, epeidē oliga men ēsthie, pleista d’ emochthei, ēuxato tōi Dii hōste tou kēpōrou apallageis heterōi apempolēthēnai despotēi.
sentences.l: A donkey serving a gardener, since he ate little but toiled very much, prayed to Zeus that, released from the gardener, he might be sold off to another master.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the little he ate against the much he laboured; the pairing is so common in Greek that it hardly needs a 'but' in English, but here the contrast is the whole grievance. ὥστε with the infinitive after a verb of praying gives the content of the prayer. ἀπαλλαγείς takes the genitive of what one is rid of.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ Διὸς ἐπακούσαντος καὶ κελεύσαντος αὐτὸν κεραμεῖ πραθῆναι, πάλιν ἐδυσφόρει, πλέον ἢ πρότερον ἀχθοφορῶν καὶ τόν τε πηλὸν καὶ τοὺς κεράμους κομίζων.
sentences.tr: Tou de Dios epakousantos kai keleusantos auton keramei prathēnai, palin edysphorei, pleon ē proteron achthophorōn kai ton te pēlon kai tous keramous komizōn.
sentences.l: And Zeus having hearkened and having ordered him to be sold to a potter, again he was aggrieved, bearing burdens more than before and carrying both the clay and the pots.
sentences.i: But when Zeus had heard him and ordered him sold to a potter, he was aggrieved again, for he bore heavier loads than before, carrying both the clay and the finished pots.
sentences.n: ἐπακούω is the word for a god's granting of a prayer — to listen and act on it, not merely to overhear. The genitive absolute τοῦ Διὸς ἐπακούσαντος καὶ κελεύσαντος carries the whole change of fortune in one clause, with the finite verb kept for the donkey's renewed grievance. The donkey now hauls both ends of the potter's trade, the wet clay in and the fired ware out.

sentences.t: Πάλιν οὖν ἀμεῖψαι τὸν δεσπότην ἱκέτευε, καὶ βυρσοδέψῃ ἀπεμπολεῖται.
sentences.tr: Palin oun ameipsai ton despotēn hiketeue, kai byrsodepsēi apempoleitai.
sentences.l: Again, then, he kept begging to change his master, and he is sold off to a tanner.
sentences.n: ἀπεμπολεῖται is a present used for a past event — the historic present, which quickens the pace just as the fable's third and worst sale arrives. The imperfect ἱκέτευε before it says the begging went on and on.

sentences.t: Εἰς χείρονα τοίνυν τῶν προτέρων δεσπότην ἐμπεσὼν καὶ ὁρῶν τὰ παρ’ αὐτοῦ πραττόμενα, μετὰ στεναγμῶν ἔφη· « Οἴμοι τῷ ταλαιπώρῳ, βέλτιον ἦν μοι παρὰ τοῖς προτέροις δεσπόταις μένειν· οὗτος γάρ, ὡς ὁρῶ, καὶ τὸ δέρμα μου κατεργάσεται. »
sentences.tr: Eis cheirona toinyn tōn proterōn despotēn empesōn kai horōn ta par’ autou prattomena, meta stenagmōn ephē· « Oimoi tōi talaipōrōi, beltion ēn moi para tois proterois despotais menein· houtos gar, hōs horō, kai to derma mou katergasetai. »
sentences.l: Having fallen, then, upon a master worse than the former ones, and seeing the things being done at his hands, with groans he said: « Alas for wretched me, it was better for me to stay with my former masters; for this one, as I see, will work up even my own hide. »
sentences.i: So, having fallen to a master worse than the earlier ones, and seeing what went on at his hands, he groaned and said: « Alas for me, poor wretch — better for me to have stayed with my earlier masters; for this one, I can see, will work up even my own skin. »
sentences.n: βέλτιον ἦν is the imperfect of unfulfilled possibility: Greek states flatly 'it was better' where English needs 'it would have been better'. Οἴμοι takes a dative of the person pitied, here the speaker himself. κατεργάζομαι is to work raw material up into a finished thing, and of a hide that means turning it into leather — which is the point of the last line: the donkey has been sold to the one trade that has a use for him dead.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τότε μάλιστα τοὺς προτέρους δεσπότας οἱ οἰκέται ποθοῦσιν, ὅταν τῶν δευτέρων λάβωσι πεῖραν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tote malista tous proterous despotas hoi oiketai pothousin, hotan tōn deuterōn labōsi peiran.
sentences.l: The fable shows that household slaves long for their former masters most of all then, when they have made trial of the later ones.
sentences.n: τότε … ὅταν is a correlative pair, 'then … when'; English drops the first half. πεῖραν λαβεῖν with the genitive is 'make trial of'. οἰκέται are the slaves of a household, and the moral is spoken from their side of the door.
